extracted.intended_audience: general readers; researchers of comedy history; comedians studying one-liner performance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive features for performing short, rapid one-line jokes in a stand-up/vaudeville style as exemplified by Henny Youngman. Covers joke form, pacing, prop use, stage length, and professional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the one-liner
rubrics_metrics.description: Was famous for his mastery of the 'one-liner', his best known being 'Take my wife... please'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine consisted of telling simple one-liner jokes, occasionally with interludes of violin playing. Examples include: 'A doctor gave his patient six months to live... but he couldn't pay his bill, so he gave him another six months.' and 'My wife's purse was stolen, but I didn't cancel her credit cards. Why should I? The guy who stole 'em spends less than she does!'

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate lengthy build-ups; go straight to the punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: His routines depicted simple, cartoon-like situations, eliminating lengthy build-ups and going straight to the punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with anecdotal, story-based comedy; the one-liner form focuses on immediacy of setup-to-punch. Youngman's sets delivered dozens of such jokes in short time windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: High joke density / rapid succession
rubrics_metrics.description: A stage performance by Youngman lasted only 15 to 20 minutes but contained dozens of jokes in rapid succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pacing and tempo are crucial — many brief jokes back-to-back rather than long narratives. This creates a barrage effect where volume of jokes is part of the comedic appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a trademark prop and musical interludes
rubrics_metrics.description: He performed while holding his trademark prop of a violin and bow, occasionally playing a short interlude of 'Smoke Gets In Your Eyes' on the violin in between jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prop/musical bits serve as a rhythmic or tonal bridge between jokes and become part of a comedian's persona; Youngman used the violin as a recognizable trademark and occasional break in his rapid one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoffensive, friendly style
rubrics_metrics.description: His inoffensive, friendly style of comedy kept his audiences laughing for decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content tended toward light, domestic humor (e.g., jokes about his wife) rather than edgy or confrontational material. Maintaining a likeable stage persona and not appearing aloof were part of his long-term appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and earning-first approach ('nem di gelt')
rubrics_metrics.description: He treated his profession as a working job where making a living is difficult and getting paid for the work is all-important, advising others 'nem di gelt' (Yiddish for 'take the money').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical career habits: perform often (as many as 200 shows per year), accept a wide range of venues (from major TV to small banquet rooms), negotiate fees, and prioritize consistent work over prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short set length and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage performances were short (15–20 minutes) and densely packed with jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designing a short, tightly-edited set that showcases many one-liners can maximize audience impact in constrained time slots (club spots, TV inserts, banquet appearances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature joke origin and repeated use
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic line 'Take my wife, please' originated from a misinterpreted stage direction and Youngman used the line countless times thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A memorable signature line or gag, even if accidental in origin, can become an identifying hook for a performer and be reused across appearances to audience recognition effect.
